title: Hauntings & Halloween / Apports & Anomalies
byline: Coast to Coast AM Staff - October 18, 2026
excerpt: Psychic medium Ericka Boussarhane discussed the origins of Halloween traditions and her experiences communicating with spirits. Followed by journalist Keith Thompson on reports of anomalous phenomena and the evidence challenging conventional scientific explanations.
content:
Guest host Richard Syrett welcomed psychic medium and paranormal investigator Ericka Boussarhane to discuss Halloween's ancient origins, tracing its traditions to the Celtic festival of Samhain, when communities gathered around bonfires, celebrated the harvest, and made offerings to deities in hopes of surviving the winter. She explained that people believed the boundary between the living and the dead became thinner during this period, allowing encounters with deceased ancestors and other spirits. According to Boussarhane, many familiar Halloween customs evolved from these beliefs, including disguises intended to confuse or avoid spirits, jack-o'-lanterns inspired by the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, and trick-or-treating rooted in medieval practices of offering prayers for the dead in exchange for food. She spoke about the holiday's associations with witches, black cats, bats, and divination, as well as Christianity's incorporation of pagan traditions into All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day.

Boussarhane also described her personal experiences as a psychic medium, recalling childhood episodes in which she believed she traveled outside her body, saw deceased individuals at her bedside, perceived colorful auras, and sensed information about people without knowing how. Growing up in a family familiar with paranormal experiences, she said these abilities initially seemed normal to her. She explained that spirit communication can involve clairvoyance, clairaudience, intuitive feelings, dreams, and mental impressions, though she also claims to experience physical apparitions and audible voices. Describing spirits as energetic beings no longer possessing physical bodies, she discussed purported paranormal encounters involving trees, historic locations, and technology that she believes can detect spiritual presences. Boussarhane emphasized that deceased loved ones are not confined to cemeteries but can visit people wherever they are, and she believes spirits can come and go freely.

------------------------------------------

Investigative journalist Keith Thompson delved into his latest book, Anomalous Phenomena: Apports and the Mystery of Objects That Materialize and Translocate, which explores unexplained events that challenge conventional understandings of consciousness and physical reality. Thompson focused on the Scole Experiment, a series of more than 400 séances conducted over five years in England during the 1990s, where participants reported mysterious lights, disembodied voices, physical contact with unseen entities, and apports, objects that seemingly materialize or move between locations through unexplained means. He described accounts of coins, a historical newspaper, and other objects appearing unexpectedly, along with unexplained images developing on photographic film. Thompson maintained that outside investigators, including members of the Society for Psychical Research, lent credibility to the experiments, although skeptics questioned the darkened conditions and the potential for deception.

Thompson recounted the experiences of a Texas family whose three-year-old son reportedly dreamed of a deceased great-grandfather he had never met, leading to a series of unusual events involving a family property, apparent spirit communication, and UFO sightings. He suggested these experiences might reflect interconnected aspects of a broader paranormal reality that current scientific theories cannot adequately explain. Sharing his own experiences, Thompson described a near-death episode while swimming off Hawaii in which he believed he left his body, encountered deceased relatives, and experienced profound serenity. He also recalled witnessing mist-like human figures and hearing what he described as celestial music during his mother's final moments, an experience he said was later echoed by a hospice nurse familiar with similar accounts. Drawing on philosopher William James's concept of radical empiricism, Thompson advocated investigating extraordinary claims with an open but critical mind, arguing that credible evidence should be examined rather than dismissed simply because it conflicts with established scientific assumptions.
